records.sourceFile: Comparison of eccentric hamstring strength and asymmetry at return-to-sport after hamstring strain injury among those who did and did not re-inj.pdf

paper.citation: Kocak UZ, Stiffler-Joachim MR, Heiderscheit BC. Comparison of eccentric hamstring strength and asymmetry at return-to-sport after hamstring strain injury among those who did and did not re-injure. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2023;59:25-29.
paper.abstract: Study of 60 NCAA Division I athletes with an index hamstring strain injury, comparing eccentric hamstring strength and between-limb asymmetry at return to sport between athletes who did and did not re-injure within 1 and 3 months. The authors found no differences in strength or asymmetry between groups and conclude that these measures at return to sport do not distinguish athletes who re-injure.
paper.tldr: In 60 collegiate athletes returning from a hamstring strain, eccentric strength and between-limb asymmetry at return to sport did not differ between those who re-injured within three months and those who did not. Only 11 athletes re-injured, so the results argue against using a single return-to-sport strength value alone to predict re-injury.
paper.methods: Analysis of routinely collected Division I health and performance records (July 2017 to March 2020), with injuries captured in a larger prospective observational study, for athletes with an index hamstring strain who were tested on a NordBord at return to sport. Peak eccentric force for each limb, total force and between-limb asymmetry were compared with Mann-Whitney U tests between athletes who did and did not re-injure the same limb within 1 and 3 months, with injury severity grouped by days to return.
paper.findings: Eight athletes (13%) re-injured within 1 month and 11 (18%) within 3 months, and none of the 11 women re-injured. Peak eccentric force (injured limb, uninjured limb and total) and asymmetry did not differ between groups at either time point (asymmetry median 8.2% vs 7.8% at 1 month and 8.3% vs 7.1% at 3 months). Re-injuries occurred in moderate-severity injuries (8 of 38 within 1 month and 10 of 38 within 3 months) and in one severe injury within 3 months, and no mild-injury athlete was re-injured.
paper.limitations: The study uses routinely collected data, with strength testing timed inconsistently after return (mean 6.8 days, typically within 7 days) and no complete injury history, and re-injury counts are small (8 and 11). Results and tables disagree: the text gives p = 0.49 and 0.48 for the moderate-severity comparisons while Table 3 gives 0.89 and 0.79, and the text gives asymmetry p values of 0.43 or above while the abstract and Table 2 give 0.91 and 0.96. The paper labels itself cross-sectional, although it follows athletes forward for re-injury, which is a cohort design.
paper.practicalImplications: A single eccentric strength or asymmetry value at return to sport should not be used on its own to decide that an athlete is at lower or higher re-injury risk, since this study found no difference between athletes who did and did not re-injure. The authors suggest eccentric strength can still be used to track strength development after injury, which is a monitoring use rather than a risk-screening use.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not measure performance outcomes. Its only performance-relevant content is the authors' suggestion that eccentric strength can monitor strength development in injured athletes.
paper.rtp: This is the study's setting. Eccentric strength and between-limb asymmetry measured at return to sport did not separate athletes who re-injured from those who did not within one or three months, so these values should not be used alone to judge re-injury risk at return. Re-injury occurred in the moderate-severity group (21% within 1 month, 26% within 3 months) and in one severe injury at 3 months, and the comparison within the moderate group was not significant.

records.sourceFile: Concussion recovery time, return-to-play protocols, and mandated sit-out periods among adult amateur contact field sports - A systematic review.pdf

paper.citation: Power LC, Kenny IC, Zynda AJ, Mulvihill JJE, Collins MW, Kontos AP, et al. Concussion recovery time, return-to-play protocols, and mandated sit-out periods among adult amateur contact field sports: A systematic review. Irish Journal of Medical Science. 2026; online.
paper.abstract: This systematic review compared sport-related concussion recovery times, return-to-play protocols and mandated sit-out periods across adult amateur contact field sports. Nineteen studies with 58 datasets were included, and the authors found wide variation between and within sports. The most common protocol was 7 days and the most common sit-out rule was no same-day return, and the authors conclude that recovery time should be read in light of sport type and local policy.
paper.tldr: Recovery times after concussion in adult amateur contact sports vary widely, and the authors suggest the sport's return-to-play and sit-out rules may shape the reported figures. Staff should not quote one sport's recovery time as a typical return date for their athletes.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA and PERSiST guidance. MEDLINE, CINAHL Complete, SPORTDiscus, APA PsycInfo and APA PsycArticles were searched on 13 May 2024 for English-language, peer-reviewed studies from 2015 to 2024 of adults in amateur field-based contact sports with recovery time data. One reviewer screened titles and abstracts, two did full-text review, one extracted data, and one rated risk of bias (NIH tool) and certainty (SORT).
paper.findings: Nineteen of 6,085 records (under 1%) met criteria, covering 58 datasets. Median recovery ranged from 6.5 days (male soccer, n = 4) to 37 days (female field hockey, n = 3, which the authors flag as a possible outlier), and rugby was consistently longer than American football (18.5 to 34 vs 7 to 16 days). Protocol duration was most often 7 days (31 of 58 datasets) and the most common sit-out was no same-day return (25 of 58); only rugby and ladies Gaelic football had extended sit-out periods (11 to 21 days), with rugby union longest at 21 days.
paper.limitations: The authors note limited study quality (six studies at level 3 evidence and eight rated fair), very small samples in some codes, only one study each for ladies Gaelic football and sprint football, and that protocol and sit-out rules had to be interpreted by the first author. The abstract and results disagree: the abstract gives 34 days as the longest field hockey recovery while Table 3 gives a 37-day median, and the abstract gives 10/19 American football and 9/19 lacrosse studies while the results give 11/19 and 9/15.
paper.practicalImplications: When setting expectations for amateur adult players after concussion, staff should check which return-to-play protocol and sit-out rule applies to that sport and league. Recovery times reported from another sport or policy should not be transferred directly.
paper.athleteDev: For performance and strength staff, the paper suggests that return times in adult amateur sport may depend on the rules and medical support in place, so training reintroduction should follow the medical clearance process in that setting. The paper does not assess training or performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: This paper is directly about return to play: median return times ranged from 6.5 to 37 days by dataset, with protocols of 5 to 21 days and sit-out periods from no same-day return to 21 days. The authors caution that policies vary, were often interpreted by the reviewer, and that compliance and medical access were rarely reported, so the figures describe published policy and outcomes, not a rule to apply to an individual athlete.

records.sourceFile: Criteria for Progressing        Rehabilitation and Determining Returnto-Play Clearance Following      Hamstring   Strain Injury- A Systematic Review.pdf

paper.citation: Hickey JT, Timmins RG, Maniar N, Williams MD, Opar DA. Criteria for Progressing Rehabilitation and Determining Return-to-Play Clearance Following Hamstring Strain Injury: A Systematic Review. Sports Med. 2017;47:1375-1387.
paper.abstract: Nine studies with 601 athletes who had acute hamstring strain injury were reviewed. Rehabilitation progression was largely guided by pain, and clinical assessments and performance tests were the most common return-to-play criteria. Isokinetic dynamometry was linked to shorter mean return-to-play times, and the Askling H-test to lower re-injury rates. The authors call for more objective and practical criteria.
paper.tldr: Hamstring rehabilitation progression is mostly guided by pain, and return-to-play decisions usually rely on subjective clinical tests. Isokinetic testing was linked to shorter return-to-play times, and the Askling H-test to fewer re-injuries, but both findings need confirmation.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA, searching six databases from inception to July 2015. Studies were included if they reported acute hamstring strain injury diagnosed within 10 days, described rehabilitation progression and return-to-play criteria, and reported return-to-play time and re-injury rates with at least 6 months of follow-up. Methodological quality was rated with a modified Downs and Black checklist.
paper.findings: Nine studies with 601 participants were included, mostly male (80.6 percent) and drawn from professional, collegiate and recreational sport. Rehabilitation was kept within pain-free limits in six studies. The most common return-to-play categories were clinical assessments (eight studies) and performance tests (seven studies), while isokinetic dynamometry was used in three studies and the Askling H-test in two. Mean return-to-play times were 12 to 25 days with isokinetic dynamometry and 36 to 63 days with the H-test. Re-injury rates were 1.3 to 3.6 percent with the H-test and 6.25 to 13.9 percent with isokinetic dynamometry, and 9.1 to 63.3 percent in the clinical and performance test studies.
paper.limitations: The review pooled return-to-play times and re-injury rates regardless of injury type, severity and rehabilitation approach. Definitions of return-to-play and follow-up periods varied. The authors state that the categories were chosen by them, and that the search was limited to English-language articles.
paper.practicalImplications: Return-to-play decisions for hamstring strain should not rely only on manual strength tests and pain-free status. The authors suggest more objective strength measures, such as isokinetic or hand-held dynamometry, while noting that isokinetic testing has limited ability to predict individual re-injury risk and that the H-test may lower re-injury but lengthens time to return. Staff should weigh return-to-play time against re-injury risk for each athlete.
paper.athleteDev: The paper addresses return-to-play criteria, not training. It notes that the performance tests used to clear athletes show readiness for sport but do not directly measure the known risk factors for re-injury, such as eccentric hamstring strength.
paper.rtp: This review directly addresses return to play after acute hamstring strain. It supports pain-free progression as the common practice but finds that most clearance criteria are subjective, and that isokinetic dynamometry and the Askling H-test are associated with different trade-offs between time to return and re-injury. The authors call for more objective and practical criteria rather than naming a validated one.

records.sourceFile: Criteria for return to running after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction- a scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Rambaud AJM, Ardern CL, Thoreux P, Regnaux JP, Edouard P. Criteria for return to running after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a scoping review. Br J Sports Med. 2018.
paper.abstract: This scoping review of 201 studies found that time was the most frequently reported criterion for returning to running after primary anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. The median time was 12 postoperative weeks. Fewer than one in five studies reported clinical, strength or performance-based criteria, and the authors recommend combining performance-based and time-based criteria.
paper.tldr: Most ACL reconstruction protocols clear athletes to run based on time alone, with a median of 12 weeks. Only a minority of studies used clinical, strength or performance criteria, and the authors suggest adding those to time-based decisions.
paper.methods: Scoping review following the Arksey and O'Malley and Joanna Briggs Institute frameworks. Six electronic databases were searched in November 2016, with reference list screening and forward citation tracking. Two reviewers screened and extracted data independently. Included studies were skeletally mature patients with primary autograft ACL reconstruction, and the review included all study designs. Time criteria were summarized as median and IQR, and trends over time were examined with local regression.
paper.findings: Of 201 included studies, 198 reported a time criterion, and the median time to permit running was 12 postoperative weeks (IQR 3.3). Open surgery with protective rehabilitation had a median of 29 weeks and arthroscopic surgery with protective rehabilitation 21 weeks, while under contemporary rehabilitation the medians were 10 and 12 weeks. Thirty-six studies (18 percent) used specific clinical, strength or performance criteria: 20 used clinical criteria, 30 strength criteria and 13 performance-based criteria. The most common objective strength criteria were isometric quadriceps limb symmetry index above 80 percent and isokinetic quadriceps and hamstring limb symmetry index above 70 percent.
paper.limitations: Time criteria are general milestones reported by study authors and do not show when each patient actually started running, and definitions of running differed across studies. Included sources ranged from trials to rehabilitation protocols and clinical commentaries, were not appraised for risk of bias, and the review did not assess whether running at 12 weeks was safe. Some counts differ between the results and discussion (strength criteria 30 vs 31 studies; performance-based criteria 13 vs 17 articles).
paper.practicalImplications: Running after ACL reconstruction should not be cleared on time alone. Staff could combine a time milestone with set criteria such as full knee extension, pain below 2 out of 10, no effusion, and knee flexion range near the uninjured side, plus strength and hop-test limb symmetry where available. The authors suggest that criteria be individualized rather than applied as a fixed timeline.
paper.athleteDev: Performance-based criteria such as single-leg squats, step-ups, and balance tests can show movement quality before running, and the authors note these tests can double as rehabilitation exercises. The review gives no evidence that any specific threshold improves later performance.
paper.rtp: This review directly addresses the transition to running, which is an early step of return to sport after ACL reconstruction. It does not establish that a given criterion or time point is safe, so it should not be used alone to clear an athlete to run; the authors recommend combining time with clinical, strength and performance criteria.

records.sourceFile: Criteria-based return to sport   decision making following lateral ankle sprain injury - A systematic  review  and narrative synthesis.pdf

paper.citation: Tassignon B, Verschueren J, Delahunt E, Smith M, Vicenzino B, Verhagen E, et al. Criteria-Based Return to Sport Decision-Making Following Lateral Ankle Sprain Injury: a Systematic Review and Narrative Synthesis. Sports Med. 2019;49:601-619.
paper.abstract: No prospective studies were found that applied a criteria-based return-to-sport decision process after lateral ankle sprain, so no pooled analysis was possible. The authors provide a narrative synthesis of questionnaires and clinical and functional tests used in ankle sprain research. They propose that complex systems theory and the return-to-sport continuum could guide development of a criteria-based decision paradigm, and they advise against time-based decisions.
paper.tldr: No published study has used criteria to clear patients with ankle sprains to return to sport. The authors suggest a multifactorial framework combining clinical, functional, sport-specific and psychosocial measures, but its criteria are untested.
paper.methods: Systematic review with a protocol registered with PROSPERO and developed in line with PRISMA-P. Seven databases were searched from inception to 23 November 2018, with reference list screening, and two reviewers screened titles, abstracts and full texts. Eligible studies prospectively applied a criteria-based return-to-sport process in adults with lateral ankle sprain. Because none qualified, the authors built an inventory of questionnaires and tests from the screened literature and wrote a narrative synthesis.
paper.findings: Of 948 articles identified, 33 were assessed in full and none met the eligibility criteria. The authors extracted 47 questionnaires, 45 clinical and functional tests, and four criteria from the wider ankle sprain literature. Only one study applied criteria, a limb symmetry index of at least 80 percent on triple hop tests, but it was excluded because it judged return after the athletes had already returned to sport. The authors report that return-to-sport decisions after ankle sprain are generally time-based.
paper.limitations: The review found no direct evidence on criteria-based decisions, so the proposed variables are a theoretical synthesis linked to tests used in ankle rehabilitation. The authors state that these variables must be applied to actual return-to-sport decisions in prospective studies, and only articles published in peer-reviewed journals were considered.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should not assume a validated criteria-based return-to-sport standard exists for ankle sprains. In the meantime, the authors suggest that clinicians consider a combination of clinical measures (ankle laxity, pain and swelling), functional and sport-specific tests, load monitoring, and psychological readiness, rather than time alone. Staff should treat the framework as a discussion aid, not a clearance protocol.
paper.athleteDev: The authors suggest that sport-specific performance profiles, movement quality, fatigue, and acute to chronic workload ratios could inform progression toward full performance. These are proposals from the synthesis, not tested training outcomes.
paper.rtp: This review directly addresses return to sport after lateral ankle sprain. It does not supply validated criteria, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete. Its main value is in highlighting that time-based decisions are common and that criteria-based decisions remain untested.

records.sourceFile: Current concepts in Achilles tendon ruptures.pdf

paper.citation: Ivanova VS, Tong KPS, Neagu C, King CM. Current Concepts in Achilles Tendon Ruptures. Clin Podiatr Med Surg. 2024;41:153-168.
paper.abstract: Acute Achilles tendon ruptures can be treated without surgery or with surgery, and both pathways use functional rehabilitation with early range of motion. Surgical options include percutaneous, minimally invasive and open repair, and recent literature reports low complication rates and similar functional outcomes. The review also covers tendon anatomy and blood supply, gap-distance measurement, a phased rehabilitation protocol and chronic rupture repair.
paper.tldr: Acute Achilles ruptures can be managed with or without surgery, and both routes use early functional rehabilitation with weight-bearing. Recent comparisons show similar re-rupture rates, so the choice depends on the patient, the rupture and the surgeon.
paper.methods: This narrative review summarises the anatomy, diagnosis, conservative and surgical treatment of Achilles tendon ruptures, and presents the authors' Kaiser Permanente early functional rehabilitation protocol (Table 1). No systematic search method is described.
paper.findings: Recent studies cited show similar re-rupture rates for surgical and nonsurgical care when early range of motion and weight-bearing are used. Minimally invasive repair had lower wound and infection rates than open repair in the pooled data cited (deep infection 2.20% vs 5.11%), but a higher risk of sural nerve injury. In one cohort of 82 patients, a plantarflexion gap over 5 mm predicted lower patient-reported outcomes, whereas a case series of 56 found no such link when the gap was measured in neutral.
paper.limitations: This is a narrative review with no described search, so selection and weighting of studies cannot be verified. Several cited figures come from older trials or from populations that are not athlete-specific, and the review does not grade the strength of the evidence.
paper.practicalImplications: The review supports early functional rehabilitation with weight-bearing whether or not surgery is performed, and stresses early diagnosis. The authors state that open repair is well accepted for chronic ruptures and for acute ruptures in young, healthy, athletic patients, while the choice of procedure otherwise depends on the surgeon and patient.
paper.athleteDev: The review touches on performance only briefly. It notes that soleus atrophy and loss of end-range plantar flexion torque are common after rupture and can limit return to activity. It gives no training or performance guidance.
paper.rtp: The return-to-sport content comes from the authors' clinic protocol (Table 1): 90% limb symmetry on single-leg heel raise and single-leg hop for distance before running, and a 90% drop countermovement jump symmetry plus a declined heel raise before unrestricted sport in the 6-month phase. The protocol is presented as clinical practice and its criteria are not tested against outcomes. In a cited WNBA cohort, 23.5% of players did not return to the sport after the injury.

records.sourceFile: Determinants of return to play after the nonoperative   management of hamstring injuries in athletes - A systematic   review.pdf

paper.citation: Fournier-Farley C, Lamontagne M, Gendron P, Gagnon DH. Determinants of Return to Play After the Nonoperative Management of Hamstring Injuries in Athletes: A Systematic Review. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016;44(8):2166-2172.
paper.abstract: This systematic review summarises the factors that influence return to play after nonoperative management of hamstring injuries in athletes. Clinical, MRI and ultrasound prognostic factors and rehabilitation approaches were reviewed. Several factors were linked to longer recovery, and two rehabilitation approaches were linked to shorter rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: Stretching-type injuries, structural injury on imaging, greater range-of-motion deficit and delayed first consultation were linked to longer return to play. The evidence is mostly low-level, so these factors guide prognosis rather than fixed timelines.
paper.methods: Systematic review following PRISMA guidance. Four databases (CINAHL, MEDLINE, Embase, EBM Reviews) were searched in June 2014, with reference-list checks. Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts, and 24 studies were included. Study quality was rated with Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine levels.
paper.findings: Clinical factors linked to longer recovery included stretching-type injury, recreational-level sport, structural rather than functional injury, a larger range-of-motion deficit, first consultation more than 1 week after injury, higher pain scores and more than 1 day to walk pain free. On MRI, positive findings, higher injury grade, more than 75% muscle involvement and proximal tendon involvement were among factors linked to longer recovery. In one level 2 study, hamstring loading during extensive lengthening (L-protocol) shortened rehabilitation compared with conventional exercise, and in another, four daily static stretching sessions shortened rehabilitation compared with one; the authors note conflicting results between studies for several factors.
paper.limitations: Only 4 of the 24 studies were randomised trials, and most were level 4 evidence. Diagnosis criteria, outcome measures and populations varied widely, and only English and French articles were included. The authors note that these factors need stronger evidence before they can be used to improve clinical decisions.
paper.practicalImplications: Record the injury type (stretching or sprinting), pain score, time to first consultation and time to walk pain free after an acute hamstring injury, since these were linked to longer recovery. Treat these as prognostic signals that flag athletes who may need a longer timeline, not as fixed return dates. The rehabilitation findings support considering loaded lengthening, but rest on a small number of studies.
paper.athleteDev: This review cannot inform performance programming. Its rehabilitation findings on loaded lengthening exercise come from injured athletes, and the review measures no performance outcomes.
paper.rtp: Use the prognostic factors (stretching-type injury, structural injury on MRI or ultrasound, range-of-motion deficit, pain, delayed first consultation) to flag athletes who may need a longer timeline. The review gives no return-to-play criteria or validated thresholds, and most factors come from single studies with inconsistent results, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete to return.

records.sourceFile: Do Self‑Myofascial Release Devices Release Myofascia Rolling Mechanisms- A Narrative Review.pdf

paper.citation: Behm DG, Wilke J. Do Self-Myofascial Release Devices Release Myofascia? Rolling Mechanisms: A Narrative Review. Sports Medicine. 2019;49:1173-1181.
paper.abstract: This narrative review argues that the term 'self-myofascial release' is misleading for foam rollers and similar devices. The authors find insufficient evidence that releasing myofascial restrictions is the primary mechanism behind range of motion and pain changes, and describe neural, pain-modulatory, circulatory and local thixotropic alternatives.
paper.tldr: Foam rolling and roller massage increase short-term range of motion and reduce pain sensitivity, but the authors argue that breaking up adhesions is unlikely to be the main reason. Neural and pain-modulation mechanisms fit the evidence better, so the term self-myofascial release should be used with caution.
paper.methods: Narrative review of the literature on foam rollers, roller massagers and balls, covering trigger point evidence, tissue stiffness and blood flow studies, non-local (contralateral) rolling effects, and the mechanical plausibility of tissue release. The authors cite PubMed title and abstract hit counts for 'self-myofascial release' (25 since 2005) and 'foam roller' or 'roller massage' (48, 2005 to 2019) to show how common the term is. No systematic search strategy or quality appraisal is reported.
paper.findings: In one study, four 45 s rolling bouts reduced anterior thigh stiffness by 15% to 24%, and another found a 13% reduction in iliotibial band stiffness at 30 minutes in experienced users only. Rolling the untreated leg reduced pain sensitivity in three studies, which the authors read as a global pain-modulatory response. The authors also cite estimates that the force needed to break up adhesions would exceed what most people can apply with a roller.
paper.limitations: The review is narrative, reports no systematic search or appraisal, and its main conclusion rests on the authors' interpretation of mostly small studies. One range of motion study had 13 participants per group and no significant between-group difference. Most trials included healthy active participants, which the authors note may not reflect people with pain.
paper.practicalImplications: Foam rolling can be used for short-term gains in range of motion and reduced pain sensitivity, since these effects are reported more consistently than tissue release. Because the review points to neural and global mechanisms, staff should not explain rolling to athletes as a way to break up adhesions. One cited study found that 60, 90 and 120 s of rolling between sets of knee extensions all reduced repetitions (by 8 to 14%), so rolling between working sets may cost performance.
paper.athleteDev: The review cites studies in which rolling did not typically impair subsequent strength, jump height, sprint time or endurance, so rolling before training is a reasonable choice when a range-of-motion gain is wanted. Some studies report improvements in strength, power or sprint speed, but the review also cites a meta-analysis describing performance and recovery effects as generally small to negligible.
paper.rtp: The review covers mechanisms in mostly healthy participants and does not assess rehabilitation outcomes or return-to-sport decisions. It cannot show that rolling restores tissue or supports return to sport. The authors call for trials in patients and athletes with pain syndromes.
